drivers.evidence: Easter week (2026-03-30) had same price ($3.46), sold at x1.12 vs baseline. No promotion, so demand was above baseline, but not due to price. Post-promotion weeks show x0.93. No prior price-only weeks with demand drop, but 6% price increase with no incentive likely suppresses demand. Noise-adjusted

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 61.3. The price is raised to $3.46 (+6.1% vs regular $3.26), which historically has suppressed demand. Past promotions show a median lift of x1.56, but noise-adjusted is x1.36. However, this week has no promotion, only a price increase. The most relevant past week with a price hike was Easter (2026-03-30), which sold at x1.12 vs baseline. The week after that, sales dropped to baseline. Given no promotion, the price increase likely reduces demand. The historical price sensitivity is not strong, but a 6.1% increase without a promotion suggests a mild downside. Confidence is medium due to limited past price-only events.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 61.3 | 5%-95%: 37.5 - 112.4 | 10%-90%: 41.7 - 95.9

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
